rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 - two-year (2018-2019) replicated field experiments at Zhengzhou and TandoJam with measured soil water, soil nitrate, LAI, dry matter and grain yield, used to calibrate (2018) and validate (2019) the WHCNS model (Section 3.1, Table 3). Q2: Section 3.2, 3.3 and Table 4 - at Zhengzhou, drip irrigation (DI) used 45 mm per season versus 120 mm under farmer flood irrigation (FI), i.e. 62.5% less irrigation water (measured by separate water meters), and WUE was 3.4 and 3.2 kg m-3 under DI versus 2.6 and 2.7 kg m-3 under FI, order DI > FI > RF; abstract reports WUE improved up to 24.5%. Q4: Table 4 and Section 3.3 - the model (validated on measured soil water) partitioned ET, showing FI soil evaporation of 195.9 mm versus 147.0 mm under DI (33% higher under FI) with near-equal transpiration (190.3 vs 193.0 mm), and drainage/runoff reduced to negligible amounts under DI (1 mm vs 20 mm average drainage); Conclusions state DI conserved water by decreasing evaporation, drainage and runoff.
rows.notes: Drip vs flood was tested only at the Zhengzhou site on maize (one soil, one climate); the TandoJam site compared deficit flood levels, not drip. Water saving is directly measured (water meters); WUE depends on simulated ET from a calibrated/validated model, but is not a second independent method. No explicit limitations of the authors' own results are stated and no SD/CI is given for WUE or irrigation amounts (only per-year values and ANOVA/LSD for yield). The explanation that benefits stem from keeping root-zone water at an optimal level is attributed to literature, not stated as a requirement from own findings.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 and 3.1 - two-year replicated field experiments (RCBD, four replications at Zhengzhou) with measured grain yield, LAI and dry matter, plus WHCNS model calibration/validation. Q2: Section 3.2 and Fig. 3 - at Zhengzhou, DI produced a significantly (p<0.05) higher two-year total grain yield of 22,449 kg ha-1 versus 20,434 kg ha-1 under farmer flood irrigation, a 9.8% increase; Conclusions state DI would significantly improve yield compared with full flood irrigation. Q4: Sections 2.1, 2.3, 3.2, Table 3 and Fig. 3 - root-zone soil water content (0-80 cm) was measured weekly and kept at 50-80% of field capacity under DI, and LAI and dry matter were measured at growth stages; the authors attribute the DI yield gain to vigorous growth, higher biomass accumulation and grain filling, with Discussion 4.1 linking it to FI inducing supersaturated topsoil and lack of air.
rows.notes: Yield effect of drip vs flood is shown at one site (Zhengzhou, maize, sandy clay loam) only; TandoJam treatments were deficit flood irrigation. Measured and simulated yields are not independent methods (the model was calibrated on the measured data). Significance via ANOVA/LSD only; no SD or CI reported in text or Table; Fig. 3 error bars cannot be verified from the text. No stated limitations of the authors' own result and no condition stated from own findings as a requirement for the yield gain.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Supplementary Fig. S1 not available. Both drip claims rest on a single-site (Zhengzhou) comparison of DI vs FI vs RF over two seasons; the Pakistan site tested deficit flood irrigation rather than drip and does not bear on the drip claims.
